text: Poliomyelitis, commonly known as polio, is an infectious disease caused by the poliovirus. Approximately 75% of cases are asymptomatic; mild symptoms such as sore throat and fever may occur in about 25% of cases and typically resolve within one or two weeks. In about 1% of infections, the virus spreads to the central nervous system (CNS), leading to nonparalytic aseptic meningitis with symptoms like headache, neck stiffness, fever, and vomiting, while in one to five in 1,000 cases, it progresses to paralytic disease, characterized by muscle weakness, floppiness, and paralysis—known as acute flaccid paralysis—most commonly affecting the legs, though it may also involve the head, neck, or diaphragm. Paralytic polio is classified as spinal, bulbar, or bulbospinal, depending on the CNS region affected; spinal polio results from damage to motor neurons in the spinal cord’s anterior horn, leading to muscle weakness and atrophy; bulbar polio affects the brain stem, causing difficulties with breathing, swallowing, and speech; and bulbospinal polio involves both bulbar and spinal regions, often resulting in diaphragm paralysis and respiratory failure. Between 2 and 10% of those with paralysis die due to respiratory complications. The disease is caused by infection with one of three serotypes of poliovirus—WPV1, WPV2, and WPV3—each with a distinct capsid protein, with WPV1 being the most commonly associated with paralysis. WPV2 was certified eradicated in 2015 and WPV3 in 2019. Polio occurs only in humans and spreads through fecal–oral or oral–oral routes, with transmission possible for up to six weeks after infection, even in asymptomatic individuals. The incubation period ranges from three to six days for nonparalytic cases and seven to 21 days if paralysis develops. The virus enters via the mouth, binds to CD155 receptors on cells, replicates in the gastrointestinal tract, and spreads to lymphoid tissues before entering the bloodstream, where it may circulate for up to 17 weeks. In rare cases, it invades the CNS, which is likely a chance event unrelated to age or socioeconomic status. Immunity develops through infection or vaccination, with IgA antibodies blocking replication in the gut and IgG and IgM preventing spread to motor neurons; however, immunity to one serotype does not protect against others. Two types of vaccines are used: the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), developed by Jonas Salk in 1952 and administered by injection, and the oral polio vaccine (OPV), introduced in 1961 and containing weakened live virus, which can be transmitted to others and, in low-vaccination settings, may revert to a virulent form, leading to circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV). An improved oral vaccine, nOPV2, with greater genetic stability, was granted full licensure and prequalification by the World Health Organization in December 2023. The global incidence of wild polio has dropped dramatically from an estimated 350,000 cases in 1988 to 30 confirmed cases in 2022, confined to Pakistan and Afghanistan as of October 2023. The term "poliomyelitis" comes from Ancient Greek, meaning inflammation of the spinal cord’s grey matter, first used in 1874 by Adolf Kussmaul, and the abbreviated term "polio" first appeared in 1911. Polio does not affect any species other than humans and is caused by a member of the Enterovirus genus. A rare condition, nonpoliovirus poliomyelitis, can result from other enteroviruses. Risk factors include pregnancy, being very young or old, immune deficiency, and malnutrition; maternal antibodies provide passive immunity to infants. Laboratory diagnosis involves detecting the virus in feces or pharyngeal swabs, or in blood or cerebrospinal fluid, with RT-PCR or genomic sequencing used to determine serotype and strain. In 1950, William Hammon developed a gamma globulin therapy from polio survivor plasma, which was about 80% effective in preventing paralytic polio and reducing disease severity, though its limited supply led to the focus on vaccine development. Both IPV and OPV are effective in providing lifelong protection and are used globally to prevent polio.

In 1950, William Hammon at the University of Pittsburgh purified the gamma globulin component from the blood plasma of polio survivors, proposing that it contained antibodies to poliovirus and could halt infection, prevent disease, and reduce its severity in other patients. A large clinical trial showed the gamma globulin was about 80 percent effective in preventing paralytic poliomyelitis and reduced disease severity in those who developed polio. However, due to limited blood plasma supply, it was deemed impractical for widespread use, leading the medical community to focus on developing a polio vaccine. Two types of polio vaccines are used globally: an inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) given by injection, developed in 1952 by Jonas Salk at the University of Pittsburgh and announced on 12 April 1955, which uses poliovirus grown in monkey kidney tissue culture (vero cell line) and chemically inactivated with formalin; after two doses, 90 percent or more of individuals develop protective antibodies to all three serotypes, and at least 99 percent are immune after three doses. Albert Sabin developed an oral polio vaccine (OPV) comprising a live, attenuated virus produced by repeated passage through nonhuman cells at subphysiological temperatures; the vaccine replicates efficiently in the gut but not in nervous system tissue. A single dose of Sabin’s trivalent OPV produces immunity in about 50 percent of recipients, and three doses provide protective antibodies in over 95 percent. Human trials began in 1957, and in 1958, the US National Institutes of Health selected it over other live attenuated vaccines; it was licensed in 1962 and became the only oral polio vaccine used worldwide. OPV efficiently blocks person-to-person transmission via oral–oral and fecal–oral routes, providing both individual and community immunity, while IPV confers good immunity but is less effective at preventing fecal–oral spread. OPV is preferred in many countries due to its low cost, ease of administration, and strong intestinal immunity, especially in endemic areas. However, on rare occasions, the attenuated virus in Sabin’s OPV can revert to a virulent form, leading to vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV); in 2017, cVDPV cases outnumbered wild poliovirus cases for the first time due to declining wild polio cases. Most industrialized countries have switched to IPV, which cannot revert, either alone or in combination with OPV. An improved oral vaccine, novel oral polio vaccine type 2 (nOPV2), began development in 2011, received emergency licensing in 2021, and full licensure in December 2023; it has greater genetic stability and is less likely to revert. There is no cure for polio; treatment focuses on symptom relief, speeding recovery, and preventing complications, including antibiotics, analgesics, moderate exercise, and a nutritious diet. Long-term rehabilitation involving occupational therapy, physical therapy, braces, corrective shoes, and orthopedic surgery is often required. Portable ventilators may be needed; historically, iron lungs were used to support breathing during acute infection until patients could breathe independently (typically one to two weeks), but their use is now largely obsolete due to advances in therapy and polio’s eradication. Other historical treatments include hydrotherapy, electrotherapy, massage, passive motion, and surgical interventions such as tendon lengthening and nerve grafting. Patients with abortive polio recover completely; those with aseptic meningitis experience symptoms lasting two to ten days followed by full recovery. In spinal polio, if nerve cells are completely destroyed, paralysis is permanent; if not, temporary loss of function may recover within four to six weeks. Half of spinal polio patients recover fully, one-quarter with mild disability, and one-quarter with severe disability. The degree of acute and residual paralysis is proportional to viremia and inversely proportional to immunity. Spinal polio is rarely fatal; without respiratory support, suffocation or pneumonia from aspiration can occur, with 5 to 10 percent of paralytic polio patients dying, and case fatality rates ranging from 2–5 percent in children to 15–30 percent in adults. Bulbar polio is often fatal without respiratory support, with CFR ranging from 25 to 75 percent depending on age, reducible to 15 percent with intermittent positive pressure ventilation. Many cases result in temporary paralysis; nerve impulses return within a month, and recovery is complete in six to eight months. Recovery involves nerve terminal sprouting, where remaining motor neurons form new branches to reinnervate denervated muscle fibers, increasing the number of muscle cells controlled by a single neuron. Other mechanisms include myofiber hypertrophy and transformation of type II to type I muscle fibers. The body compensates for residual paralysis by using weaker muscles at higher intensity, developing little-used muscles, and using ligaments for stability. Residual complications include skeletal deformities, joint tightening, and movement disability; equinus foot occurs when downward-pulling muscles work but upward-pulling ones do not, leading to a foot that drops and retracts Achilles tendons, impairing walking. If one leg grows slower than the other, it causes limb length discrepancy and spinal deformities like scoliosis; interventions include epiphysiodesis or custom footwear. Prolonged immobility can lead to pulmonary edema, aspiration pneumonia, urinary tract infections, kidney stones, paralytic ileus, myocarditis, and cor pulmonale. Between 25 and 50 percent of individuals who recovered from paralytic polio in childhood develop post-polio syndrome (PPS) decades later, characterized by new muscle weakness and extreme fatigue, thought to result from failure of oversized motor units created during recovery. Contributing factors include aging, permanent residual impairment, and overuse or disuse of neurons; PPS is progressive and has no specific treatment. Paralysis and limb length differences impair gait, and orthotics—such as stance phase control knee joints—can improve walking by providing mechanical support and enabling a natural gait pattern. Locked knee joints prevent flexion during swing phase, requiring compensatory mechanisms like Duchenne limping or circumduction. Polio epidemics were unknown before the 20th century; prior to that, it was an endemic disease worldwide. Mothers who survived polio passed temporary immunity to their babies in utero and through breast milk, so infants generally had mild symptoms and long-term immunity. Improvements in sanitation during the 19th century reduced herd immunity, leading to frequent epidemics, which killed or paralyzed over half a million people annually. After widespread vaccine use in the mid-1950s, polio cases declined dramatically in industrialized nations. Global eradication efforts began in 1988, led by the World Health Organization, UNICEF, and The Rotary Foundation, and are ongoing. Polio is one of only two diseases under a global eradication program, the other being Guinea worm disease. Smallpox and rinderpest are the only diseases completely eradicated by humans; smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980, rinderpest in 2011. In April 2012, the World Health Assembly declared failure to eradicate polio a programmatic emergency and stated it "must not happen." Efforts have greatly reduced cases, from 350,000 in 1988 to 483 in 2001, then stabilizing at about 1,000–2,000 annually. By 2015, wild polio remained in only Pakistan and Afghanistan, with outbreaks in neighboring countries due to hidden or re-established transmission. Global surveillance includes testing acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) cases and environmental/wastewater samples to detect circulating virus. The last region with wild polio is South Asia, specifically Afghanistan and Pakistan. In 2011, the CIA ran a fake hepatitis vaccination clinic in Abbottabad, Pakistan, damaging trust in vaccination programs; 66 vaccinators were killed in 2013 and 2014. In Afghanistan, the Taliban banned house-to-house polio vaccination from 2018 to 2021, hindering eradication efforts. In Afghanistan, polio cases dropped from 80 in 2011 to 4 in 2021. In Pakistan, cases fell by 97 percent from 2014 to 2018, due to a 440 million dirham donation from the UAE, changes in military conditions, and arrests of attackers. The Americas were declared polio-free in 1994, with the last known case in Peru in 1991. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends polio boosters for travelers and residents in endemic areas. In July 2022, New York reported its first polio case in nearly a decade, attributed to a vaccine-derived strain. In 2000, polio was declared eliminated in 37 Western Pacific countries, including China and Australia. Despite eradication, an outbreak involving a Pakistan strain was confirmed in China in September 2011. In September 2019, the Philippines declared a polio outbreak after a single case in a 3-year-old girl.

The Americas were declared polio-free in 1994, with the last known case occurring in a boy in Peru in 1991. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends polio vaccination boosters for travelers and individuals living in countries where the disease is endemic. In July 2022, New York reported its first polio case in nearly a decade, attributed to a vaccine-derived strain. In 2000, polio was officially eliminated in 37 Western Pacific countries, including China and Australia. Despite eradication ten years earlier, China experienced an outbreak in September 2011 involving a strain common in Pakistan. In September 2019, the Philippines declared a polio outbreak after a single case in a 3-year-old girl, and in December 2019, acute poliomyelitis was confirmed in an infant in Sabah, Malaysia, with three additional cases reported, the last in January 2020; both outbreaks were linked to vaccine-derived poliomyelitis. Europe was declared polio-free in 2002. On 27 March 2014, the WHO announced the eradication of poliomyelitis in the South-East Asia Region, which includes Bangladesh, Bhutan, North Korea, India, Indonesia, Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Thailand, and Timor-Leste, bringing 80% of the world population into polio-free regions. As of January 2023, Syria is considered polio-free but remains at high risk for imported outbreaks; difficulties in immunization programs during the civil war led to a return of wild polio in 2012–2013, with 15 cases confirmed in Deir Ezzor between October and November 2013, and two more cases in rural Damascus and Aleppo; a vaccination campaign conducted under gunfire resulted in the deaths of several vaccinators but restored pre-war vaccination coverage; an outbreak in 2017 was caused by circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2, both of which were contained through intensive vaccination and surveillance. In 2022, before the Israel-Hamas conflict, routine immunization coverage in Israel exceeded 99%, but fell to less than 90% by the first quarter of 2024, according to the WHO; in 2024, the Gaza Health Ministry reported symptoms consistent with polio in several children, with laboratory confirmation of a 10-month-old child infected; United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres called for a weeklong cease-fire to enable vaccinations and prevent a potential outbreak. In 2003, a fatwa in northern Nigeria declared the polio vaccine designed to render children sterile, leading to polio's reappearance and spread to other countries; in 2013, nine health workers administering the vaccine were killed in Kano, though this was the only attack; local traditional and religious leaders and polio survivors helped revive the campaign, and Nigeria was removed from the polio-endemic list in September 2015 after over a year without cases, only to be restored in 2016 after two cases were detected. Africa was declared free of wild polio in August 2020, though circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 continues to appear in several countries; a single wild polio case in Malawi in February 2022 and another in Mozambique in May 2022, both imported from Pakistan, do not affect Africa’s wild poliovirus-free status. Polio’s effects have been known since prehistory, with Egyptian art depicting people with withered limbs and children using canes; the earliest known case is from a 4000-year-old burial site in the UAE involving a teenage girl. The first clinical description was by English physician Michael Underwood in 1789, who referred to it as "a debility of the lower extremities"; it was later known as Heine–Medin disease due to the work of Jakob Heine in 1840 and Karl Oskar Medin in 1890, and called infantile paralysis due to its effect on children. Before the 20th century, polio infections were rare in infants under six months, mostly affecting children aged six months to four years; poor sanitation led to constant exposure and natural immunity, but improvements in sanitation in developed countries during the late 19th and early 20th centuries reduced childhood exposure and immunity, increasing risk of paralytic polio. Small paralytic epidemics began in Europe and the US around 1900, reaching pandemic levels in Europe, North America, Australia, and New Zealand during the first half of the 20th century; by 1950, the peak age incidence in the US shifted to children aged five to nine, with about one-third of cases in persons over 15; the 1952 epidemic was the worst in US history, with nearly 58,000 cases, 3,145 deaths, and 21,269 left with mild to disabling paralysis; intensive care medicine originated in the fight against polio, with respiratory centers established in 1952 at Blegdam Hospital in Copenhagen by Bjørn Ibsen, who later founded the world’s first dedicated ICU. Polio epidemics altered lives and brought cultural changes, including grassroots fundraising and the development of rehabilitation therapy; polio survivors helped advance the disability rights movement, with the WHO estimating 10 to 20 million survivors worldwide; in 1977, 254,000 US residents were paralyzed by polio; in 2001, estimates showed 40,000 survivors in Germany, 30,000 in Japan, 24,000 in France, 16,000 in Australia, 12,000 in Canada, and 12,000 in the UK; many notable individuals credit polio with shaping their careers. The disease was widely publicized in the 1950s, and 15 scientists and two laymen who contributed to polio research are honored in the Polio Hall of Fame, established in 1957 at the Roosevelt Warm Springs Institute for Rehabilitation, with four organizations—Rotary International, WHO, CDC, and UNICEF—added in 2008. World Polio Day (24 October) was established by Rotary International to commemorate the birth of Jonas Salk, who led the first team to develop a polio vaccine. The Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI), launched in 1988 by WHO, UNICEF, and The Rotary Foundation, has reduced polio worldwide by 99 percent and continues. In 2010, wild poliovirus was detected through importation in 13 countries: Chad, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Republic of Congo, Kazakhstan, Liberia, Mali, Nepal, Niger, the Russian Federation, Senegal, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uganda. In 2021, types 2 and 3 were fully eradicated globally, though type 1 cases still persist in Pakistan and Afghanistan; these two countries remain the only ones with endemic poliovirus. Countries considered polio-free but not confirmed as of April 2024 include Somalia, Djibouti, Sudan, Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Morocco, Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman, Yemen, the UAE, Iraq, Kuwait, and Iran. Since 2018, GPEI has coordinated efforts to eliminate polio and improve surveillance and prevention, employing 4,000 people across 75 countries and managing a budget of nearly US $1 billion. As of 2021, GPEI had raised 18 billion dollars in funding, with annual contributions between 800 million and 1 billion dollars; approximately 30% came from the Gates Foundation, 30% from developed governments, 27% from polio-risk countries, and the remainder from nonprofits, private funders, and other foundations. GPEI has identified six research directions, including continuing vaccination programs for at least ten years after eradication and gradually reducing the retention of live poliovirus samples in laboratories and manufacturing facilities due to escape risks; vaccines under development use virus-like particles or modified viruses that cannot reproduce in humans.
